chunks: We were told by Muhammad ibn Ali Majilawayh, from his paternal uncle Muhammad ibn Abi'l-Qasem, from Muhammad ibn Ali al-Kufi, from Musa ibn Sa'dan, from Abdullah ibn al-Qasem, from Abdullah ibn Sinan, that he said:

Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: There is no valid oath in anger, nor in coercion, nor in compulsion. I said: May Allah rectify you, then what is the difference between compulsion and coercion? He said: Coercion is from the ruler, and compulsion is from a wife, mother and father, and is nothing.
ai.seo_question: What is the difference between coercion and compulsion in Shia jurisprudence regarding oaths?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) establishes that oaths taken under duress are invalid, distinguishing between 'ijbar' (coercion by a ruler or authority) and 'ikrah' (compulsion by family members). He rules that compulsion by parents or spouses is insignificant, reflecting the Shia juristic view that familial pressure does not carry the same legal weight as authoritative force in nullifying vows. This distinction highlights the nuanced understanding of social hierarchy and authority in early Islamic society.
